screens.title: Deploying Fabric Components with Docker Compose
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to convert a network design into a working docker-compose. yaml that starts CAs, Orderers, Peers, and CouchDB for local development. Docker Compose acts as a single blueprint: services, networks, and volumes declared in one file produce the same multi-container environment each time you run it. You'll see not just which images to use, but the important configuration pieces: environment variables for identity and TLS, volume mounts for ledger persistence, and a dedicated Docker network so Fabric components discover each other by service name. I'll also show how a CLI service can be included so you execute peer and orderer commands from a reproducible container context. Practical issues matter here — mismapped volumes or missing MSP paths are common reasons containers fail to initialize — so we cover quick troubleshooting checks and the typical docker-compose commands you'll use frequently. By the end you should be able to draft a compose file for a two-organization, single-orderer network, start it, and know where to look when containers report errors. Think of this as building a local lab: repeatable, inspectable, and a safe space to test chaincode and channel operations.

Deploying Fabric Components with Docker Compose

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter focuses on practical skills you need to deploy a local Hyperledger Fabric network using Docker Compose. First, you'll translate a conceptual network into a docker-compose. yaml that lists services, networks, and volumes; this is essential because the YAML is the reproducible blueprint teams share. Second, you'll configure service-level details: environment variables for MSP and TLS, volume mounts for ledger persistence, and ports for access. Third, you will define and use a dedicated Docker network so components can discover each other by name while remaining isolated. Finally, you will start, stop, and clean the network using docker-compose commands and learn common troubleshooting checks. For example, when a peer reports missing ledger data, you'll learn to inspect volume mounts and container paths. Each objective couples a hands-on action with the reason it matters in development: reproducibility, correct identity and TLS setup, secure inter-container communication, and reliable cleanup. These skills let you build a two-org, single-orderer lab and iterate quickly without risking stale state or misconfigured services.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Hands-on Focus
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond configuration, this chapter targets hands-on operations you'll repeat in every Fabric lab. You'll create a two-organization, one-orderer compose file that includes CAs, Peers, CouchDB instances, and a CLI container for orchestration tasks. You'll practice binding host directories as volumes so crypto material and ledger state persist across container restarts. You'll test name-based service discovery using a dedicated Docker network and verify that peers can contact the orderer and CAs. You will also learn to stop and tear down networks cleanly, using down with the volumes flag to remove persistent data when you need a fresh start. The activity walks you step-by-step through a sample file structure and the commands to run, and it asks you to reason about failures: when a peer doesn't find ledger data it often points to an incorrect host path or a mismatch between declared volume names and mount points inside the container. These operational skills make local development reliable and reproducible for team collaboration.

screens.title: Docker Compose as a Fabric blueprint
screens.narratorSegment: Docker Compose serves as the single source of truth for a local Fabric deployment. In plain terms, the docker-compose. yaml lists the services — CAs, Orderers, Peers, CouchDB, and CLI — and the networks and volumes they use. This matters because Fabric is a multi-component system: without a single coordinated configuration, teams get drift where containers start with inconsistent environment variables, different image versions, or mismatched volume paths. A compose file enforces a consistent topology and gives you explicit declarations for three essential areas: service images and commands, environment variables that establish MSP IDs and TLS configuration, and volume mounts that persist crypto material and ledger data. For example, declaring a peer service with CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS ensures that the peer advertises the right identity and is reachable by other services on the same Docker network. A common misconception is that docker-compose is only for convenience; in Fabric workflows it is also about reproducibility and repeatable testability. When you version-control the YAML alongside scripts that generate crypto artifacts and channel artifacts, you create a lab that any team member can start with docker-compose up -d and expect the same behavior. As a practical check, always run docker-compose ps and docker-compose logs to confirm services reached their ready state, and verify that volumes were created as declared.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Docker Compose as a Blueprint
Definition and role
Compose defines services, networks, and volumes in one YAML file so the entire Fabric network can be started and stopped reliably on a single host.
  • • Services: the containers for orderer, peer, CA, couchdb, and CLI.
  • • Networks: named Docker networks for secure inter-service communication.
  • • Volumes: persistent storage for crypto material and ledgers.
Concrete example
Declaring CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID=Org1MSP and a volume for /var/hyperledger/production lets the peer present the right identity and keep ledger data across restarts.
Practical checklist when authoring a compose file
Images & versions
Pin Fabric images to compatible versions for your Fabric release to avoid runtime incompatibilities.
Environment variables
Set MSP IDs, addresses, and TLS settings so services initialize with the right identity and endpoints.
Volumes
Map host paths for MSP, TLS, and ledger directories to container paths like /var/hyperledger/production.
Network
Declare a network such as basic-fabric-net and attach all Fabric services to it for name resolution and isolation.
Common mistake
Forgetting to mount the peer's /var/hyperledger/production volume causes ledger initialization errors. Double-check host paths and permissions.
Key takeaway
Design the compose file for repeatability: explicit env variables, pinned images, and declared volumes and networks.

screens.title: Defining Docker networks for Fabric
screens.narratorSegment: A dedicated Docker network is essential for local Fabric deployments because it enables name-based discovery and logical isolation. When you declare networks: basic-fabric-net: in your compose file and assign every Fabric service to that network, containers can reference each other by service names such as peer0. org1. example. com or orderer. ordererorg. example. com. This avoids brittle IP addresses and simplifies inter-service communication. The process to design the network starts with choosing a single network for the Fabric components on a host. Next, add that network to each service definition so DNS resolution works. Finally, avoid attaching unrelated host containers to that network unless they are explicitly part of the Fabric lab. A common pattern is to set the network name in the top-level networks block and then reference it under each service. Misconceptions include thinking port mappings provide internal connectivity; ports only expose services to the host and other networks — they do not replace a compose network for internal name resolution. For multi-host production you need a different orchestration solution, but for single-host development a single dedicated network reduces configuration friction and keeps the test network isolated.

keyIdea.title: Network = name resolution + isolation
keyIdea.text: Declare and reuse a named Docker network in your compose file so Fabric services resolve by name and stay isolated from unrelated host containers.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Defining Docker networks
Process: Create and assign a dedicated network
Three-step pattern for reliable service discovery and isolation.
1
Declare the network
Add a top-level networks: basic-fabric-net: entry. This gives a name you can reference across services.
2
Attach services
Under each service add networks: - basic-fabric-net so containers join the same overlay for DNS resolution.
3
Limit exposure
Only map ports required for external access; do not expose internal-only ports unnecessarily.
Why not only use ports?
Ports map to the host, but they do not provide internal DNS. Peers use peer service names to communicate; networks enable that discovery.
Quick verification
After docker-compose up -d, run docker-compose ps and then docker exec into a peer container to ping the orderer by its service name. If resolution fails, check the networks section.
Key takeaway
Use a named network in compose for reliable name resolution and isolation of Fabric components on a single host.

screens.title: Configuring a Fabric CA service
screens.narratorSegment: A Fabric Certificate Authority (CA) issues certificates for identities and stores its data persistently. In a compose file the CA service typically uses the hyperledger/fabric-ca image, exposes its port like 7054, mounts a directory for its server state, and sets environment variables that control identity and TLS behavior. Important environment variables include FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME, which defines where the CA writes its database and crypto material inside the container, FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED to toggle TLS, and FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CSR_CN to set the common name used in the certificate signing request. You must map a host directory to the container path specified by FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME so the CA can persist its ca-server. db and crypto files across restarts. A common error is to declare FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME but forget to create or mount the corresponding host path; the CA will fail when it cannot create its database. Another pitfall is mismatching host permissions: the container must be able to write the mounted path. As an example, mapping./crypto-config/org1/ca:/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server matches the typical file layout used by Fabric samples and makes subsequent certificate enrollment and artifact generation predictable for CLI operations. Configuring a Fabric CA service means set fabric_ca_server_home and mount the same host path so the ca can persist ca-server.db and crypto material across container restarts.. In practical terms, key environment variables, ports, and volume mounts for the ca. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Configuring a Fabric CA
CA service essentials
Image, port, volumes and environment variables matter for CA operations.
  • • Image: hyperledger/fabric-ca:latest (pin versions for release compatibility).
  • • Ports: expose 7054 for enrollment and admin operations.
  • • Volumes: mount a host path to FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME so ca-server.db persists.
  • • Env: FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED, FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CA_NAME, and FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CSR_CN.
Common mistake
Missing or incorrect volume mapping for FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME prevents the CA from creating its database and crypto files.
Concrete scenario
You declare FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME=/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server inside the container and mount ./crypto-config/org1/ca:/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server on the host. This lets you run enroll and identity commands from the CLI container against a persistent CA store.
Key takeaway
Map the declared FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME to a host path with correct permissions so enrollment and certificate issuance work reliably.

screens.title: Orderer configuration in compose
screens.narratorSegment: Orderers coordinate block delivery and ordering for channels; in a compose file you define an orderer service that includes environment variables for listen address, TLS settings, and local MSP configuration. Key environment variables to set include ORDERER_GENERAL_LISTENADDRESS, ORDERER_GENERAL_LISTENPORT, ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ENABLED, ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPID, and ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPDIR. You must mount crypto material and the genesis block into the container so the orderer can bootstrap correctly. For a Raft-based development setup, include ORDERER_CONSENSUS_TYPE=raft and configure the RAFT consenters information via ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS, which points to the other orderer nodes. In a single-orderer lab you can still use raft settings but keep consenters consistent. Another important detail is setting FABRIC_CFG_PATH inside the container if you supply a custom orderer. yaml. A frequent configuration pitfall is mounting MSP and TLS directories under incorrect container paths; the orderer will not start if it cannot find its local MSP or genesis. block. During local development, mounting the ledger data to a named volume like orderer. ordererorg. example. com:/var/hyperledger/production ensures ledger persistence across restarts. Remember that production deployments use external orchestration, but compose must be precise so local tests mimic expected runtime behavior.

keyIdea.title: Orderer must find its MSP & genesis
keyIdea.text: Mount the orderer's MSP, TLS material, and genesis.block at the container paths the orderer expects, and set ORDERER_* env vars for identity and TLS.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Orderer configuration
Orderer: what to declare
Ensure the orderer finds its local MSP, TLS certs, and genesis block at runtime.
Essential env vars
ORDERER_GENERAL_LISTENPORT, ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ENABLED, ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPID, ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPDIR.
Volumes
Mount MSP and tls directories and channel-artifacts/genesis.block into /etc/hyperledger/fabric within the container.
Raft consideration
If using Raft, set ORDERER_CONSENSUS_TYPE=raft and declare ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS consistently across orderer services.
Concrete example
Mount ./crypto-config/ordererOrganizations/ordererorg.example.com/orderers/orderer.ordererorg.example.com/msp to /etc/hyperledger/fabric/msp and map channel-artifacts/genesis.block to /etc/hyperledger/fabric/genesis.block so the orderer bootstraps properly.
Common mistake
Using the wrong container path for the genesis file or MSP directory causes the orderer to fail early with configuration or file-not-found errors.
Key takeaway
The orderer needs explicit env and mounted files. Confirm container paths and genesis placement before starting the network.

screens.title: Peer service configuration and CouchDB
screens.narratorSegment: Peers are the workhorses that host ledgers and endorse transactions. In compose, a peer service typically uses hyperledger/fabric-peer and includes a set of environment variables that tell it about its local MSP, gossip behavior, chaincode settings, and state database. Key variables include CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, CORE_PEER_GOSSIP_EXTERNALENDPOINT, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE, and the CouchDB address and credentials if using CouchDB. If you choose CouchDB as the state database, declare a separate couchdb service with hyperledger/fabric-couchdb and mount persistent volumes for its data. Then point the peer at couchdb0. org1. example. com:5984 (or the host-mapped port) in CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS. Also ensure peers mount /var/hyperledger/production to a named volume for ledger persistence. A frequent misconception is that chaincode will run without configuring CORE_VM_ENDPOINT and chaincode addresses; for chaincode container invocation to work, peers must be able to launch chaincode containers or connect to external chaincode runtimes. During development, using the peer's default Docker mode requires mapping /var/run/docker. sock so the peer can start chaincode containers on the host. Verify that the CouchDB container is healthy before peer startup; peers often depend on CouchDB to initialize state database connections.

keyIdea.title: Peer + CouchDB configs
keyIdea.text: Set CORE_PEER_* env variables, mount production volumes, and declare a CouchDB service if you use document state persistence.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Peer configuration & CouchDB
Peer configuration essentials
Peers need environment variables for identity, gossip, and the ledger's state database.
  • • CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID: the peer's MSP identity.
  • • CORE_PEER_ADDRESS and CORE_PEER_LISTENADDRESS: where the peer listens and how it advertises itself.
  • • CORE_PEER_GOSSIP_EXTERNALENDPOINT: crucial for cross-host discovery in compose networks.
  • • CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE=CouchDB and related CouchDB address/credentials.
CouchDB service
Run hyperledger/fabric-couchdb, mount a named volume for /opt/couchdb/data, and set COUCHDB_USER and COUCHDB_PASSWORD. Point peers at its service name and port.
Concrete example
Set CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS=couchdb0.org1.example.com:5984 and CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_USERNAME=admin with matching couchdb envs. Ensure couchdb starts before the peer by using depends_on in compose.
Common mistake
Not mapping /var/run/docker.sock prevents the peer from launching chaincode containers in default dev mode; provide the mount if you intend to run chaincode this way.
Key takeaway
Peers require precise env variables and persistent volumes; CouchDB must be reachable and healthy before peer initialization.

keyIdea.text: A clear compose structure lists networks first, then services, and finally volumes; mirror the sample layout and adapt host paths and image tags.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Starter docker-compose.yaml
Starter structure (fill in details)
version: '3.7'

networks:
  basic-fabric-net:
    name: basic-fabric-net

services:
  ca.org1.example.com:
    image: hyperledger/fabric-ca:latest
    environment:
      - FABRIC_CA_HOME=/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server
      - FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED=true
    ports:
      - "8054:7054"
    volumes:
      - ./crypto-config/peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/ca:/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server
    networks:
      - basic-fabric-net

  peer0.org1.example.com:
    image: hyperledger/fabric-peer:latest
    environment:
      - CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID=Org1MSP
      - CORE_PEER_ADDRESS=peer0.org1.example.com:7051
      - CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE=CouchDB
    depends_on:
      - couchdb0.org1.example.com
    networks:
      - basic-fabric-net

  couchdb0.org1.example.com:
    image: hyperledger/fabric-couchdb:latest
    environment:
      - COUCHDB_USER=admin
      - COUCHDB_PASSWORD=password
    networks:
      - basic-fabric-net

volumes:
  peer0.org1.example.com:
  couchdb0.org1.example.com:
Use this skeleton as a baseline. Replace latest with pinned versions before sharing in a team environment.
Example guidance
  • • Ensure service names match the hostnames referenced in crypto material.
  • • Use depends_on to prefer start order, but verify readiness via logs or health checks.
  • • Declare named volumes at the bottom to prevent ambiguous anonymous volumes.
Key takeaway
A readable compose skeleton speeds development: start with a template, then adapt volumes, networks, and pinned images to your environment.

screens.title: Lifecycle: up, ps, logs, down
screens.narratorSegment: Running and managing a local Fabric network is a repeatable workflow: start services, inspect status, read logs for issues, and tear down cleanly. The primary commands you'll use are docker-compose up -d to start containers in detached mode, docker-compose ps to list running services and their ports, and docker-compose logs -f to follow output while services initialize. When you need a clean slate, docker-compose down --volumes --remove-orphans removes containers and associated named volumes and eliminates stray containers not defined in the current compose file. This is important because Fabric ledger and CouchDB data persist in volumes; if you want to rebuild channels or reset state you must remove those volumes intentionally. A common misconception is relying solely on docker rm and docker rmi; compose down with volume removal handles related volumes and avoids leaving orphaned data. When you run into startup issues, the logs will reveal common causes: permission errors on mounted host directories, missing files like genesis. block, or environment variable typos. Use docker-compose ps to confirm service names and ports and docker-compose logs to find the first failing subsystem, then cross-check your compose file volume and env settings.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Lifecycle: up, ps, logs, down
Common commands
Your daily workflow for starting and managing a Fabric compose network.
  1. 1) docker-compose up -d: starts all services in detached mode so your terminal remains free for other tasks.
  2. 2) docker-compose ps: lists services, containers, and exposed ports to confirm expected state.
  3. 3) docker-compose logs -f : follow logs to see initialization steps and errors in real time.
  4. 4) docker-compose down --volumes --remove-orphans: tear down containers and remove named volumes to reset state.
Troubleshooting pattern
Check logs for permission or file-not-found errors, then verify volume mounts and environment variables before rerunning the compose lifecycle.
Scenario: Resetting a lab
If you want a fresh ledger, run docker-compose down --volumes --remove-orphans, then optionally remove named volumes using docker volume ls and docker volume rm if necessary.
Key takeaway
Follow the lifecycle pattern and remove volumes intentionally when you need a clean state; logs are your primary diagnostic tool.

screens.title: Integrating a CLI service
screens.narratorSegment: Including a CLI container in your compose file gives you a reproducible environment to run peer and orderer CLI commands without depending on host-installed tooling. The CLI service typically uses hyperledger/fabric-tools and mounts the same crypto-config and channel-artifacts directories used by the orderer and peers. Configuration includes CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, and ORDERER_ADDRESS so the CLI knows which peer and orderer to contact by default. By mounting crypto material, you avoid copy-paste and keep certificates and MSP directories synchronized across containers. The CLI is useful for generating genesis and channel artifacts, creating channels, joining peers to channels, installing and instantiating chaincode, and issuing enrollment operations against CAs. A common pitfall is using different file paths in the CLI volume mounts than those declared for peers; keep mounts consistent so the CLI finds the expected MSP and tls materials. Use docker-compose exec cli to run commands within the CLI container. This approach increases repeatability and reduces differences between team members' local shells and environments. Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Integrating a CLI service
Why include a CLI container?
It ensures everyone runs peer and orderer commands in the same environment with the same mounted artifacts.
• Use hyperledger/fabric-tools for the CLI image.
• Mount ./crypto-config, ./channel-artifacts, ./scripts and ./chaincode into the container.

How to run commands
Use docker-compose exec cli peer channel create or peer chaincode install from the CLI container so the operations use the exact crypto material mounted into the container.
Concrete scenario
Mount ./crypto-config into /opt/gopath/src/github.com/hyperledger/fabric/peer/crypto inside the CLI container and set CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH to point there so peer CLI commands use the expected MSP.
Key takeaway
A CLI service centralizes operations and reduces host environment differences, making lab commands reproducible across developers.

screens.title: Common failure modes and quick checks
screens.narratorSegment: When a Fabric compose deployment fails, the container logs usually point to a small set of root causes. The most common is volume mount errors: a peer or CA cannot find or write to its expected directory. Check that the host path exists, the mount target matches the environment variable path inside the container, and permissions allow the container to write. Another frequent cause is incorrect environment variables: typos in CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID or misconfigured CORE_PEER_ADDRESS cause peers to identify incorrectly or advertise wrong endpoints. Image version mismatches lead to protocol incompatibilities; ensure all Fabric images match the expected release. If CouchDB is used, ensure it started and is reachable on the configured address and port; peers that depend on CouchDB will fail initialization if they cannot connect. A practical troubleshooting sequence is: check docker-compose ps for container status, examine docker-compose logs -f for the failing service, inspect volume mounts and file ownership on the host, and finally confirm network attachment with docker network inspect. Avoid guessing: follow logs and configuration checks in that order to resolve most common problems quickly. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Failure modes & checks
Checklist for common errors
Follow this logical order to diagnose most issues when a service won't start.
1. Examine logs
docker-compose logs -f will usually point directly to missing files, permission errors, or connection failures.
2. Check volumes
Confirm host paths exist, are mounted to the expected container paths, and have writable permissions for the container user.
3. Validate env vars
Typos in CORE_* or ORDERER_* variables can break identity resolution and connections.
4. Verify network
Use docker network inspect basic-fabric-net to confirm all expected containers are members and reachable by name.
5. Confirm image versions
Ensure images like fabric-peer and fabric-orderer match the Fabric release used to generate channel artifacts.
Key takeaway
Diagnose with logs, then check mounts, env vars, network membership, and image versions in that order to resolve most startup failures.

screens.title: Volumes and persistence hierarchy
screens.narratorSegment: Persistence is critical when working with ledgers and CA stores. In compose, you typically use a mix of host-path mounts for crypto material and named volumes for container-managed data like peer production directories and CouchDB. Host-path mounts, such as./crypto-config/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com:/etc/hyperledger/fabric/msp, let you generate artifacts on the host and make them visible to containers. Named volumes like peer0. org1. example. com:/var/hyperledger/production allow Docker to manage ledger data and survive container recreation. The hierarchy to choose is: use host mounts for artifacts you edit or generate from the host, and use named volumes for runtime data that containers exclusively write to. Ensure file ownership and permissions on host mounted paths allow the container process to write; many failures stem from permission-denied errors. Another important practice is to declare volumes at the bottom of the compose file so your named volumes are explicit. When you need a fresh state, run docker-compose down --volumes to remove named volumes. Be deliberate: removing volumes deletes ledger and CouchDB data, which is often the intended step for a clean lab but disastrous if done unintentionally in a semi-production test environment.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Volumes & persistence
Volume hierarchy
Decide when to use host mounts versus named volumes.
  • • Host mounts: for crypto-config and channel-artifacts you generate or edit on the host.
  • • Named volumes: for peer ledger and CouchDB runtime data managed by Docker.
  • • Declare volumes at the bottom of docker-compose.yaml for clarity and reuse.
Permission note
Ensure host-mounted directories are writable by the container process. Permission errors are a frequent cause of startup failure.
Concrete example
Use ./crypto-config for MSP artifacts and peer0.org1.example.com:/var/hyperledger/production as a named volume. This keeps editable artifacts on the host while ledger data persists in Docker-managed storage.
Key takeaway
Map artifacts to the host when you need to work on them and use named volumes for ledger and runtime database persistence for reliability.

screens.title: Local Compose vs. Production Orchestration
screens.narratorSegment: Docker Compose is ideal for single-host development, testing, and proofs-of-concept because it provides a simple, versioned way to start all Fabric components together. It is lightweight and easy to reason about, and it maps well to developer workflows where persisting ledgers and certificates locally is convenient. However, Compose is not a production orchestration platform: it lacks built-in rollout strategies, autoscaling, and cross-host scheduling that production environments require. Kubernetes provides advanced lifecycle management, pod health checks, service discovery across nodes, and integration with cluster storage and ingress, making it the preferred choice for production-grade Fabric deployments requiring high availability and scalability. A common misconception is treating Compose deployments as production-ready simply by adding restart policies; while restart helps resilience on a single host, it doesn't solve distributed scheduling, network partitioning, or secure multi-node secrets management. For local development, use Compose to iterate quickly and validate functionality. When you need high availability or multi-host topologies, translate your architecture to Kubernetes manifests and adopt a more advanced certificate and storage strategy. Local Compose vs. Production Orchestration means use docker compose for single-host development and test; plan to migrate to kubernetes for production-scale, multi-host fabric deployments.. In practical terms, when docker compose is appropriate and when to move to kubernetes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.2 › Compose vs Kubernetes
When to use Docker Compose
Fast local iteration, single-host labs, and reproducible developer environments.
  • • Quick start and teardown for experiments.
  • • Simple file-based configuration and volume mounts.
  • • Easy to version alongside scripts and artifacts.
When to choose Kubernetes
Production needs for HA, multi-host scheduling, secrets management, and advanced networking.
  • • Automated health checks and rolling updates.
  • • Persistent storage integrated with cluster providers.
  • • Scalability across nodes and robust service discovery.
Key takeaway
Use Compose for deliberate local development and testing. Plan migrations to Kubernetes when you require high availability, scaling, or multi-host deployments.

These practices make local development reliable, repeatable, and friendly to team collaboration.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to convert a network design into a working docker-compose. yaml that starts CAs, Orderers, Peers, and CouchDB for local development. Docker Compose acts as a single blueprint: services, networks, and volumes declared in one file produce the same multi-container environment each time you run it. You'll see not just which images to use, but the important configuration pieces: environment variables for identity and TLS, volume mounts for ledger persistence, and a dedicated Docker network so Fabric components discover each other by service name. I'll also show how a CLI service can be included so you execute peer and orderer commands from a reproducible container context. Practical issues matter here — mismapped volumes or missing MSP paths are common reasons containers fail to initialize — so we cover quick troubleshooting checks and the typical docker-compose commands you'll use frequently. By the end you should be able to draft a compose file for a two-organization, single-orderer network, start it, and know where to look when containers report errors. Think of this as building a local lab: repeatable, inspectable, and a safe space to test chaincode and channel operations.

This chapter focuses on practical skills you need to deploy a local Hyperledger Fabric network using Docker Compose. First, you'll translate a conceptual network into a docker-compose. yaml that lists services, networks, and volumes; this is essential because the YAML is the reproducible blueprint teams share. Second, you'll configure service-level details: environment variables for MSP and TLS, volume mounts for ledger persistence, and ports for access. Third, you will define and use a dedicated Docker network so components can discover each other by name while remaining isolated. Docker Compose serves as the single source of truth for a local Fabric deployment. In plain terms, the docker-compose. yaml lists the services — CAs, Orderers, Peers, CouchDB, and CLI — and the networks and volumes they use. This matters because Fabric is a multi-component system: without a single coordinated configuration, teams get drift where containers start with inconsistent environment variables, different image versions, or mismatched volume paths. A compose file enforces a consistent topology and gives you explicit declarations for three essential areas: service images and commands, environment variables that establish MSP IDs and TLS configuration, and volume mounts that persist crypto material and ledger data. For example, declaring a peer service with CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID and CORE_PEER_ADDRESS ensures that the peer advertises the right identity and is reachable by other services on the same Docker network. A common misconception is that docker-compose is only for convenience; in Fabric workflows it is also about reproducibility and repeatable testability. When you version-control the YAML alongside scripts that generate crypto artifacts and channel artifacts, you create a lab that any team member can start with docker-compose up -d and expect the same behavior. As a practical check, always run docker-compose ps and docker-compose logs to confirm services reached their ready state, and verify that volumes were created as declared.

A dedicated Docker network is essential for local Fabric deployments because it enables name-based discovery and logical isolation. When you declare networks: basic-fabric-net: in your compose file and assign every Fabric service to that network, containers can reference each other by service names such as peer0. org1. example. com or orderer. ordererorg. example. com. This avoids brittle IP addresses and simplifies inter-service communication. The process to design the network starts with choosing a single network for the Fabric components on a host. Next, add that network to each service definition so DNS resolution works. Finally, avoid attaching unrelated host containers to that network unless they are explicitly part of the Fabric lab. A common pattern is to set the network name in the top-level networks block and then reference it under each service. Misconceptions include thinking port mappings provide internal connectivity; ports only expose services to the host and other networks — they do not replace a compose network for internal name resolution. For multi-host production you need a different orchestration solution, but for single-host development a single dedicated network reduces configuration friction and keeps the test network isolated.

A Fabric Certificate Authority (CA) issues certificates for identities and stores its data persistently. In a compose file the CA service typically uses the hyperledger/fabric-ca image, exposes its port like 7054, mounts a directory for its server state, and sets environment variables that control identity and TLS behavior. Important environment variables include FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME, which defines where the CA writes its database and crypto material inside the container, FABRIC_CA_SERVER_TLS_ENABLED to toggle TLS, and FABRIC_CA_SERVER_CSR_CN to set the common name used in the certificate signing request. You must map a host directory to the container path specified by FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME so the CA can persist its ca-server. db and crypto files across restarts. A common error is to declare FABRIC_CA_SERVER_HOME but forget to create or mount the corresponding host path; the CA will fail when it cannot create its database. Another pitfall is mismatching host permissions: the container must be able to write the mounted path. As an example, mapping./crypto-config/org1/ca:/etc/hyperledger/fabric-ca-server matches the typical file layout used by Fabric samples and makes subsequent certificate enrollment and artifact generation predictable for CLI operations. Configuring a Fabric CA service means set fabric_ca_server_home and mount the same host path so the ca can persist ca-server.db and crypto material across container restarts.. Orderers coordinate block delivery and ordering for channels; in a compose file you define an orderer service that includes environment variables for listen address, TLS settings, and local MSP configuration. Key environment variables to set include ORDERER_GENERAL_LISTENADDRESS, ORDERER_GENERAL_LISTENPORT, ORDERER_GENERAL_TLS_ENABLED, ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPID, and ORDERER_GENERAL_LOCALMSPDIR. You must mount crypto material and the genesis block into the container so the orderer can bootstrap correctly. For a Raft-based development setup, include ORDERER_CONSENSUS_TYPE=raft and configure the RAFT consenters information via ORDERER_CONSENSUS_RAFT_CONSENTERS, which points to the other orderer nodes. In a single-orderer lab you can still use raft settings but keep consenters consistent. Another important detail is setting FABRIC_CFG_PATH inside the container if you supply a custom orderer. yaml. A frequent configuration pitfall is mounting MSP and TLS directories under incorrect container paths; the orderer will not start if it cannot find its local MSP or genesis. block. During local development, mounting the ledger data to a named volume like orderer. ordererorg. example. com:/var/hyperledger/production ensures ledger persistence across restarts. Remember that production deployments use external orchestration, but compose must be precise so local tests mimic expected runtime behavior.

Peers are the workhorses that host ledgers and endorse transactions. In compose, a peer service typically uses hyperledger/fabric-peer and includes a set of environment variables that tell it about its local MSP, gossip behavior, chaincode settings, and state database. Key variables include CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, CORE_PEER_GOSSIP_EXTERNALENDPOINT, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_LEDGER_STATE_STATEDATABASE, and the CouchDB address and credentials if using CouchDB. If you choose CouchDB as the state database, declare a separate couchdb service with hyperledger/fabric-couchdb and mount persistent volumes for its data. Then point the peer at couchdb0. org1. example. com:5984 (or the host-mapped port) in CORE_LEDGER_STATE_COUCHDBCONFIG_COUCHDBADDRESS. Also ensure peers mount /var/hyperledger/production to a named volume for ledger persistence. A frequent misconception is that chaincode will run without configuring CORE_VM_ENDPOINT and chaincode addresses; for chaincode container invocation to work, peers must be able to launch chaincode containers or connect to external chaincode runtimes. During development, using the peer's default Docker mode requires mapping /var/run/docker. sock so the peer can start chaincode containers on the host. Verify that the CouchDB container is healthy before peer startup; peers often depend on CouchDB to initialize state database connections.

Running and managing a local Fabric network is a repeatable workflow: start services, inspect status, read logs for issues, and tear down cleanly. The primary commands you'll use are docker-compose up -d to start containers in detached mode, docker-compose ps to list running services and their ports, and docker-compose logs -f to follow output while services initialize. When you need a clean slate, docker-compose down --volumes --remove-orphans removes containers and associated named volumes and eliminates stray containers not defined in the current compose file. This is important because Fabric ledger and CouchDB data persist in volumes; if you want to rebuild channels or reset state you must remove those volumes intentionally. A common misconception is relying solely on docker rm and docker rmi; compose down with volume removal handles related volumes and avoids leaving orphaned data. When you run into startup issues, the logs will reveal common causes: permission errors on mounted host directories, missing files like genesis. block, or environment variable typos. Use docker-compose ps to confirm service names and ports and docker-compose logs to find the first failing subsystem, then cross-check your compose file volume and env settings.

Including a CLI container in your compose file gives you a reproducible environment to run peer and orderer CLI commands without depending on host-installed tooling. The CLI service typically uses hyperledger/fabric-tools and mounts the same crypto-config and channel-artifacts directories used by the orderer and peers. Configuration includes CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID, CORE_PEER_MSPCONFIGPATH, CORE_PEER_ADDRESS, and ORDERER_ADDRESS so the CLI knows which peer and orderer to contact by default. By mounting crypto material, you avoid copy-paste and keep certificates and MSP directories synchronized across containers. The CLI is useful for generating genesis and channel artifacts, creating channels, joining peers to channels, installing and instantiating chaincode, and issuing enrollment operations against CAs. A common pitfall is using different file paths in the CLI volume mounts than those declared for peers; keep mounts consistent so the CLI finds the expected MSP and tls materials. Use docker-compose exec cli to run commands within the CLI container. This approach increases repeatability and reduces differences between team members' local shells and environments. When a Fabric compose deployment fails, the container logs usually point to a small set of root causes. The most common is volume mount errors: a peer or CA cannot find or write to its expected directory. Check that the host path exists, the mount target matches the environment variable path inside the container, and permissions allow the container to write. Another frequent cause is incorrect environment variables: typos in CORE_PEER_LOCALMSPID or misconfigured CORE_PEER_ADDRESS cause peers to identify incorrectly or advertise wrong endpoints. Image version mismatches lead to protocol incompatibilities; ensure all Fabric images match the expected release. If CouchDB is used, ensure it started and is reachable on the configured address and port; peers that depend on CouchDB will fail initialization if they cannot connect. A practical troubleshooting sequence is: check docker-compose ps for container status, examine docker-compose logs -f for the failing service, inspect volume mounts and file ownership on the host, and finally confirm network attachment with docker network inspect. Avoid guessing: follow logs and configuration checks in that order to resolve most common problems quickly. Persistence is critical when working with ledgers and CA stores. In compose, you typically use a mix of host-path mounts for crypto material and named volumes for container-managed data like peer production directories and CouchDB. Host-path mounts, such as./crypto-config/peerOrganizations/org1. example. com:/etc/hyperledger/fabric/msp, let you generate artifacts on the host and make them visible to containers. Named volumes like peer0. org1. example. com:/var/hyperledger/production allow Docker to manage ledger data and survive container recreation. The hierarchy to choose is: use host mounts for artifacts you edit or generate from the host, and use named volumes for runtime data that containers exclusively write to. Ensure file ownership and permissions on host mounted paths allow the container process to write; many failures stem from permission-denied errors. Another important practice is to declare volumes at the bottom of the compose file so your named volumes are explicit. When you need a fresh state, run docker-compose down --volumes to remove named volumes. Be deliberate: removing volumes deletes ledger and CouchDB data, which is often the intended step for a clean lab but disastrous if done unintentionally in a semi-production test environment.

Docker Compose is ideal for single-host development, testing, and proofs-of-concept because it provides a simple, versioned way to start all Fabric components together. It is lightweight and easy to reason about, and it maps well to developer workflows where persisting ledgers and certificates locally is convenient. However, Compose is not a production orchestration platform: it lacks built-in rollout strategies, autoscaling, and cross-host scheduling that production environments require. Kubernetes provides advanced lifecycle management, pod health checks, service discovery across nodes, and integration with cluster storage and ingress, making it the preferred choice for production-grade Fabric deployments requiring high availability and scalability. A common misconception is treating Compose deployments as production-ready simply by adding restart policies; while restart helps resilience on a single host, it doesn't solve distributed scheduling, network partitioning, or secure multi-node secrets management. For local development, use Compose to iterate quickly and validate functionality. When you need high availability or multi-host topologies, translate your architecture to Kubernetes manifests and adopt a more advanced certificate and storage strategy. Let's review the core ideas from this chapter. First, Docker Compose acts as a reproducible blueprint for local Fabric networks: declaring services, networks, and volumes ensures consistent start-up across machines. Second, environment variables and volume mounts are not optional; they determine MSP identity, TLS behavior, ledger persistence, and chaincode execution. Third, a dedicated Docker network gives services name-based discovery and isolates the Fabric lab from other host containers. Use named volumes for runtime data and host mounts for crypto artifacts you generate or edit. Finally, run and manage your lab with docker-compose up -d, inspect with docker-compose ps and logs, and remove state with docker-compose down --volumes when you need a clean slate. When problems occur, start with logs, then verify mounts, env variables, network membership, and image versions. These practices make local development reliable, repeatable, and friendly to team collaboration.
